endorsements.quote: Periodic audits of the models can ensure they are not disproportionately flagging one demographic or systematically overlooking certain elites.
Responsible use also entails monitoring AI performance for bias.
Legal, ethical, and operational frameworks should guide decisions about where human oversight is needed in the AI pipeline and to what extent.
Thus, if an AI application flags an official as high‐risk, there should be transparent procedures for review to enable the official to challenge the finding.

unlisted_practices: Train and retain appropriately skilled analysts and investigators for AI use.
Invest in data systems to train and apply AI algorithms.
Standardise healthcare data, enhance interoperability, and promote open data initiatives to support AI detection of corruption.
Legal frameworks should facilitate responsible data sharing for AI tools.
Governments should institutionalise successful AI tools so they persist beyond a single political administration or donor project.
Integrate AI tools into existing workflows and structures through hybrid AI-human models.
Use AI as a decision-support tool that hands top-risk items to human auditors rather than acting automatically.
Implement AI anti-corruption tools with appropriate legal frameworks, independent oversight, and stakeholder consultation.
Protect AI systems against adversarial manipulation of input data through ongoing vigilance.
Use blockchain to secure procurement records and prevent data manipulation.

screen.reason: This is a commentary/perspective article examining the opportunities and governance challenges of using AI to combat corruption and fraud in the healthcare sector.
